title: Supreme Court can restore sanity and stop the left’s radical climate agenda
text:

When the U.S. Supreme Court opens its new term on Oct. 5, the justices will face the critical question of whether Congress or Boulder, Colorado, controls American energy policy. Cities such as Boulder, Honolulu and Baltimore have pursued frivolous lawsuits against energy companies on the claim that big oil concealed the effects of their products on climate change.

While states generally set policy over public health and safety, constitutional law and Supreme Court precedent should make the answer clear. Energy forms a central part of the national economy and makes a foundational contribution to American national security. The Constitution vests authority over interstate commerce and national security in the federal government, not the states.

But until the court resolves this matter once and for all in Suncor v. Boulder, dozens of states and municipalities, backed by climate activists, will keep pushing legal theories in state court intended to impose ruinous liability on energy companies for lawful carbon emissions. Without the court’s intervention, climate litigants would sue American energy into financial oblivion, inflict enormous costs on the American economy and render the nation more vulnerable to coercion by nations such as Russia and Iran.

THESE 11 UPCOMING SUPREME COURT DECISIONS COULD MAKE OR BREAK TRUMP'S SECOND TERM AGENDA

The decisions about how to regulate carbon emissions and respond to global climate belong to the federal government, not the states or localities. Greenhouse gases do not remain within state or even national borders. Once emitted, they enter the global atmosphere. Emissions from a gas station in Boulder are functionally indistinguishable from emissions from a coal plant in another state or a factory overseas. A problem that transcends state and national borders requires a uniform national solution that includes foreign policy implications and the costs and benefits of energy for the country as a whole.

The left is going after energy companies and trying to overturn federal control. That now lands in the lap of the Supreme Court. (Astrid Riecken/Getty Images)

Courts have long recognized interstate pollution disputes as a federal domain. Before Congress legislated on the subject, the Supreme Court held that interstate water and air pollution were governed by federal common law to be created by the courts directly. It found that states have conflicting interests and that the underlying activity is national in scope. Therefore, the court concluded, there is an overriding national need for one uniform rule of decision, not 50 competing ones.

NEW YORK WANTS TO GOVERN IOWA AND MISSOURI — WE'RE SUING TO STOP IT COLD

Consider the implications of Boulder’s lawsuit. Close to 90% of global carbon emissions originate from outside the United States. The lion’s share comes from China, which accounts for close to a third of worldwide emissions alone. A Colorado state court judgment holding U.S. energy producers responsible for the world’s emissions is ultimately a tax on American energy that our international competitors do not have to pay. Good luck persuading Beijing to pay for the harms inflicted by its pollution on the rest of the world.

Energy is ultimately an instrument of power. U.S. foreign policy and national security demand a unified federal approach. Energy and climate policy are inseparable from foreign affairs. The United States has negotiated over carbon emissions for decades through climate agreements and diplomacy with allies and adversaries alike. State court rulings penalizing global emissions necessarily affect the bargaining positions and policy choices available to the federal government, whether or not any existing treaty speaks to the point directly. Reliable energy supplies are essential to military readiness and economic resilience. State courts have no authority to enter judgments on global conduct that could undercut the nation’s military posture or impair the federal government’s diplomacy.

TRUMP-APPROVED ENERGY PROJECTS AT RISK OF SUDDEN DEATH BY NEXT HOSTILE PRESIDENT

These groundless lawsuits not only interfere with national security and foreign policy, they also interfere with the federal government’s ability to effectively regulate a national industry. The energy defendants in Boulder operate lawfully, a truth the climate plaintiffs do not dispute, and already comply with federal statutes regulating carbon emissions.

In the Clean Air Act, Congress created a comprehensive regulatory structure that left states a narrow, defined role. It assigned the job of regulating global emissions to the Environmental Protection Agency, not to state court judges and juries.

The constitutional structure and design demand limits on Boulder’s authority. The Framers entrusted national institutions with interests that should not be subject to a patchwork of state laws. Foreign policy, national defense, the economy and interstate pollution remain subjects that must rest in the hands of the federal government. American energy productivity and our national security depend on each other.

Allowing Boulder’s climate suit to move forward would not only undermine the authority of Congress, but it would hand a single Colorado county control over matters that bear directly on American national security. Foreign policy decisions must not fall subject to the whims of state court juries or the climate activists who bring cases to them.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Supreme Court should hold that these questions belong to the federal government, and it should say so in no uncertain terms. Boulder’s bid to set American energy policy through climate litigation should end with Suncor. If not, activist jurisdictions will continue this lawfare campaign until American energy is bankrupt, our economy is irreparably damaged and our national security is directly undermined.

John Yoo is Heller Professor of Law at the University of California, Berkeley; distinguished visiting scholar at the School of Civic Leadership and a senior research fellow at the Civitas Institute at the University of Texas at Austin; and a nonresident senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.
